indicators.note: after says the first drug named follows the second one in the answer

parts.note: crack is a smokable form of cocaine
pot is slang for cannabis

explanation.surface: Someone is calling a person a fool for taking one drug on top of another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after' means the first drug named goes second in the answer; 'using' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words are informal names for a foolish or eccentric person, so they are synonyms.

indicators.note: in tells us one piece is placed inside the other

parts.note: real means substantial, having actual existence
mitt is slang for a hand

explanation.surface: Someone is asked to hand over a large sum of money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hand in' reads as a phrasal verb meaning submit, but the two words do separate jobs here.
explanation.definitionFit: A remittal is a sending of money, a remittance, so it is a kind of payment.

parts.note: deep thought is thinking hard with full focus; the word for that state of mind can also describe a strong, undiluted liquid, which is deep in another sense

explanation.surface: A question about what counts as profound thinking.
explanation.definitionFit: Thinking with full focus is described by the same word as a strong, dense solution, so the clue punns on both senses.

clue.text: Gone and dead in father's temple

indicators.note: in places the gone and dead pieces inside the father word

parts.note: pa is an informal word for father
ago means gone by, in the past
D is the abbreviation for dead, as in genealogies

explanation.surface: Someone has died and been laid in their father's temple.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gone' tempts you towards GO, but it means 'in the past'; 'and' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A pagoda is a tiered tower used as a Buddhist or Hindu temple in East Asia.

indicators.note: flipping means the word for notice is turned over and read backwards

parts.note: to spot is to notice

explanation.surface: Someone notices hooded youths turning somersaults.
explanation.definitionFit: Hoodies are an example of upper-body garments, so the question mark marks a definition by example.

clue.text: Object to, for example, right in shift

indicators.note: in places the example and right letters inside the shift word

parts.note: to budge is to shift slightly
EG is the abbreviation for exempli gratia, for example

explanation.surface: Someone objects, for instance, to a right being moved.
explanation.definitionFit: To grudge or resent something is to object to it, so the phrase is a synonym.

clue.text: Probability of overdose on drugs case

indicators.note: case means the outside letters of drugs, the shell around its middle

explanation.surface: A doctor estimates the likelihood of an overdose in a drugs case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' is a link: in a down answer the overdose letters sit on top of the drugs case.
explanation.definitionFit: Betting odds express the likelihood of an outcome, so the word means chance or likelihood.

clue.text: Obscene, inept nonsense about rugby union, right?

indicators.note: about means the jumbled letters wrap around the following pieces
nonsense says the word inept is jumbled into a new order

parts.note: taken as written for the anagram

explanation.surface: A complaint that a stupid, crude remark about rugby is justified.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nonsense' scrambles 'inept' into a five-letter run that 'about' then opens up around the rugby and right letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Prurient means having an excessive, unhealthy interest in sexual matters, close to lewd or indecent.

clue.text: Bush, perhaps, old chief taking note

indicators.note: taking means the chief word takes in the note letter

parts.note: a leader is a chief
N for note, as an abbreviation

explanation.surface: A former President Bush is pictured as an old leader making a note.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bush' suggests a US President, but it is a shrub, and 'perhaps' marks an example.
explanation.definitionFit: The oleander is an evergreen flowering shrub, so it is one example of a bush.

indicators.note: initially means take the opening letter of each of the four words before it

explanation.surface: Something that may make people anxious at first.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both definition and wordplay: the first letters spell the answer, and a sign of what is coming can make one nervous.
explanation.definitionFit: A portent of trouble ahead tends to make people anxious, so the whole clue describes it.

parts.note: seems to praise a sharp television picture, but TV is short for transvestite, and the clue asks for a good name for one

explanation.surface: A comment on the picture quality of a television set.
explanation.walkthrough: TV reads as television, with definition as picture sharpness; in fact TV is the abbreviation for transvestite and definition means a description.
explanation.definitionFit: TV is a common abbreviation for transvestite, a person who wears clothes of the opposite sex.

clue.text: Stupid brat's a cretin — he can't think straight

indicators.note: stupid suggests the letters are muddled and laid out in a new order

parts.note: taken as written; the apostrophe adds no letter
taken as written for the anagram

explanation.surface: An insult hurled at a dim child who cannot reason clearly.
explanation.definitionFit: A muddled, forgetful person who cannot concentrate is one who fails to think clearly.

clue.text: Street as well as a road guide

parts.note: and means as well as

explanation.surface: A street map that also covers a road, as a route guide.
explanation.definitionFit: A standard is a model or benchmark that serves as a guide for judging others.

clue.text: Little offensive between Germany and France

indicators.note: between puts the offensive word between the two country letters

parts.note: D is the international vehicle code for Germany (Deutschland)
F is the international vehicle code for France
an offensive is a military attack, so war

explanation.surface: A small military attack between Germany and France.
explanation.definitionFit: Dwarf as an adjective describes a plant or animal much smaller than usual, so tiny or small.

indicators.note: admitting means the yearn word lets the attention word inside it

parts.note: to be dying for something is to yearn, so die
to have someone's ear is to have their attention

explanation.surface: Longing that lets in attentiveness for the sake of love.
explanation.walkthrough: 'love' is not a feeling here but a term of address, like 'my dear'.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are affectionate forms of address, used as one might say 'darling' to someone.

indicators.note: endless means the drink word loses its final letter

parts.note: to slurp is to drink noisily

explanation.surface: Heavy drinking that makes speech garbled.
explanation.definitionFit: To slur speech is to run words together so they come out indistinct, to mumble or garble them.

indicators.note: in puts the money inside the mailed word

parts.note: something mailed has been sent
a dime is a US ten-cent coin

explanation.surface: US currency deposited by post.
explanation.walkthrough: 'deposit' looks like a bank payment matching the money, but it means matter settling at the bottom.
explanation.definitionFit: Sediment is matter that settles to the bottom of a liquid, a geological deposit.

clue.text: Rock fish on top of sea

indicators.note: on means the fish follows the sea letter, placed on it
top of means the opening letter of sea

parts.note: hake is a food fish

explanation.surface: A fish swimming at the sea's surface, near a rock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rock' looks like a stone, but it is a verb, to sway or jolt.
explanation.definitionFit: To rock something is to move it violently back and forth, a synonym of jolt or jar.

parts.note: to strum is to play a guitar casually
a pet is a favourite, as a teacher's pet

explanation.surface: Fooling about with a beloved pastry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tart' suggests a pastry; here it is slang for a promiscuous woman.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are dated, disparaging slang for a woman considered promiscuous, so they are synonyms.

explanation.surface: An attempt to arrange a game between nations.
explanation.definitionFit: To try is to put to a trial or examine; in cricket and rugby a full match between national teams has the same name.

clue.text: One new leader in steady, easy job

indicators.note: leader in means the pieces go inside the steady word right after its leading letter

parts.note: secure means steady, firmly fixed
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A newcomer, the first one, finds steady and undemanding work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leader in' puts I and N just after the first letter of SECURE.
explanation.definitionFit: A sinecure is a paid post that needs little or no work, from Latin for 'without care'.

indicators.note: taking means the opening word holds the scan letters inside

parts.note: a door is an opening into a room
CT is short for computed tomography, a medical scan

explanation.surface: A hospital specialist's initial appointment includes a scan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Consultant's' is the definition plus 's (is); a consultant is a senior hospital doctor in Britain. 'opening' suggests a first appointment but is DOOR.
explanation.definitionFit: In British hospitals a consultant is a senior medical specialist, so a physician.

parts.note: a standard is a banner or flag
a rant is a long angry speech, a diatribe

explanation.surface: An overt, run-of-the-mill tirade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'standard' suggests ordinary, but here it is a banner.
explanation.definitionFit: Flagrant means conspicuous and shameless, done openly rather than hidden.

explanation.surface: A question about approximately how many holes a golf course has.
explanation.definitionFit: Roughly means approximately; a golfer playing all eighteen holes completes a single circuit of the course, split as two words.

clue.text: I'm due a sermon, possibly, for transgression

indicators.note: possibly signals the letters could be arranged another way

parts.note: taken as written; the apostrophe adds no letter
taken as written for the anagram
taken as written for the anagram

explanation.surface: A sinner expects a lecture from the pulpit for wrongdoing.
explanation.definitionFit: A misdemeanour is a minor wrongdoing or offence, a kind of transgression.

explanation.surface: A massacre in which many were slain.
explanation.definitionFit: A slew is an informal word for a great quantity; slew is also the past tense of slay, to kill.

indicators.note: headless means the decline word loses its first letter

parts.note: a lapse is a decline, a falling off in standards

explanation.surface: A decapitated figure is spotted in a church in decline.
explanation.definitionFit: An apse is the vaulted semicircular recess at the east end of many churches, a feature found there.

indicators.note: up means the brass word is read the other way round

parts.note: the tuba is an instrument in the brass section

explanation.surface: An invitation to sign up as a brass band player.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Join up' reads as enlisting, but 'up' is the reversal signal and 'Join' alone defines.
explanation.definitionFit: To abut is to adjoin, to touch along a shared border.

clue.text: Head of state after winds up redundant

indicators.note: after places that letter behind the winds up word

parts.note: to wind someone up is to tease or needle them

indicators.note: head of means the opening letter of state

explanation.surface: A head of state retires after being declared surplus to requirements.
explanation.walkthrough: 'winds up' suggests ends or concludes; here it means teases.
explanation.definitionFit: Needless means unnecessary, not required, so it is a synonym of superfluous.

parts.note: death is one's end
dyspepsia, indigestion, figuratively means bad temper or irritability, hence wrath

explanation.surface: Could indigestion be life-threatening?
explanation.walkthrough: 'by' is a link; dyspepsia has an old figurative sense of ill humour, which the question mark flags.
explanation.definitionFit: To endanger is to put in peril, which is to risk something.
